summaries.example: Imagine a picture made from many tiny dots. The whole picture might look like a face or a tree, but its pattern depends on where the dots are. Physicalists use a similar idea: minds, living things, and societies may depend in important ways on physical features, even if they are not easy to describe as just one physical object.
summaries.summary: Physicalism is the view that everything is physical, or has the right kind of dependence on the physical. The view does not deny that thoughts, feelings, living things, laws, societies, and numbers appear different from ordinary physical objects. Instead, it asks how these parts of reality connect to the physical. The entry first distinguishes the completeness question—what relation everything must have to the physical—from the condition question—what counts as physical. Possible answers include supervenience, identity, realization, grounding, and fundamentality. Each has advantages and difficulties. The entry also considers whether physicalism requires reducing one science to another, whether physical truths can be known to imply all other truths, and whether consciousness, meaning, or abstract objects create problems. Finally, it presents arguments against physicalism and arguments from causal closure and scientific methods in its favor. The entry does not treat the debate as settled.
key_ideas: Physicalism is a claim about what the world is really like, not simply a claim about how we use words.
Physicalists can accept that minds, living things, rules, numbers, and societies seem different from rocks or atoms. They ask how these things relate to the physical world.
Philosophers disagree about the best relation: some discuss dependence, identity, realization, grounding, or what is fundamental.
A major challenge concerns conscious experience: knowing all the physical information might seem different from knowing what an experience feels like.
The entry separates two questions: what “physical” means and how everything must relate to the physical.
summaries.why_it_matters: Physicalism helps philosophers ask a basic question: how do minds, living things, societies, and other parts of reality fit into one world? The debate also affects how we think about consciousness and science. Learning the different proposals shows why a simple slogan such as “everything is physical” can lead to difficult questions.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical view that everything is physical, or depends in an important way on what is physical.
The idea that one set of features depends on another set so that two things cannot differ in the first set without differing in the second.
The question of what it means for something to be physical.
The question of how everything must be related to the physical if physicalism is true.
A feature of experience, such as what seeing a color feels like.

questions_to_think_about: If a thought depends on brain activity, does that make the thought physical?
Can two very different kinds of creatures have the same feeling?
Would knowing every physical fact tell someone what a color feels like?
Are numbers physical things, or do they belong to a different category?

summaries.example: Suppose two possible worlds match perfectly in every physical respect. Supervenience physicalism says they cannot differ in their psychological, biological, or social facts. But this may not be enough: a property could depend on physical facts without being physical in its own nature. This is illustrated by the contrast between Socrates and the set containing only Socrates: facts about the set depend on facts about Socrates, yet the set is not identical to Socrates. The example motivates stronger accounts than simple supervenience.
summaries.summary: Physicalism is usually presented as the metaphysical thesis that everything is physical, although “physical” and “material” have different historical associations. The entry organizes the debate around two interpretive questions. The completeness question asks what relation nonphysical-seeming features must bear to the physical; the condition question asks what makes a property physical. Supervenience physicalism says that no physical duplicate could differ in mental, biological, or social respects. Yet supervenience may be too weak, since dependence does not guarantee sameness of nature. Identity physicalism strengthens the claim, but token identity appears unable to accommodate some social objects, while type identity faces multiple realizability. Realization and grounding offer intermediate proposals, though their exact relations to supervenience remain disputed. Fundamentality accounts identify the fundamental properties with physical ones. The entry also distinguishes reductive from non-reductive physicalism and a priori from a posteriori versions. Challenges include the knowledge argument about qualia, arguments concerning meaning and intentionality, the status of abstract objects, and a methodological criticism that physicalist metaphysics may be confused with scientific naturalism. Arguments for physicalism appeal to causal closure and the methods of natural science, but the entry presents these arguments and replies as contested.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes the interpretation question from the truth question. Interpretation asks what physicalism means; truth asks whether it is correct.
The completeness question can be answered with modal ideas such as supervenience or necessity, or with non-modal ideas such as identity, realization, grounding, or fundamentality.
Supervenience appears necessary to many physicalists but may be insufficient: dependence does not by itself show that the dependent feature is physical in nature.
Identity accounts face different problems. Token identity may be too weak, while type identity may be too strong because one psychological kind might have multiple physical realizations.

Physicalism need not mean every mental concept can be translated into a physical concept, every psychological theory can be reduced to neuroscience, or every mental property is identical with a neural property.
The main objections concern qualia, intentionality, abstract objects, and methodological questions. Arguments for physicalism appeal especially to causal closure and methodological naturalism.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate concerns how consciousness, thought, biology, social institutions, mathematics, and physics belong together in one account of reality. It also clarifies what “reduction” means: physicalism need not entail that psychology is simply replaceable by neuroscience. Understanding the distinctions prevents both an oversimplified “mind is just matter” slogan and an overly quick rejection of physicalism based on one objection.

important_terms.definition: A metaphysical thesis claiming that everything is physical or stands in the required relation to the physical.
A dependence relation: no two possible worlds can match in all physical respects while differing in other relevant respects.
The view that every particular object, event, or process is identical with some physical particular.
The view that every instantiated property is identical with some physical property.
A relation in which one property fulfills the causal or theoretical role associated with another, or possesses a relevant subset of its causal powers.
A relation in which one fact or property holds in virtue of another, or is explained by it.
A property of experience considered from the first-person side, such as what a color experience feels like.
The aboutness or representational direction of a mental state, such as thinking about Vienna or believing that snow is white.

questions_to_think_about: Does supervenience capture what physicalism means, or could something nonphysical still supervene on the physical?
Does multiple realizability undermine type physicalism, or only a particular kind of reductionism?
Is knowing every physical truth enough to know what an experience feels like?
Can a theory of meaning based on dispositions explain both correct and incorrect uses of words?
Should physicalism be understood as a true metaphysical thesis, a scientific attitude, or a claim about the limits of inquiry?

summaries.example: Think about a school team. The team has rules, a name, and a history, but it is not one extra object sitting beside its players. Its features depend on people, actions, and arrangements. A physicalist might use this kind of case to ask whether a social thing can depend on physical facts without being identical to one physical object. This helps show why “depends on” and “is exactly the same as” are different ideas.
summaries.summary: Physicalism says that reality is physical, or that everything has the right kind of connection to the physical. This does not deny the existence of thoughts, feelings, organisms, social institutions, or mathematical truths. It claims that these things are not independent of the physical world in the relevant way. To explain the view, the entry separates the completeness question from the condition question. The first asks whether everything must supervene on, be identical with, be realized by, be grounded in, or be based on fundamental physical properties. The second asks what “physical” means. A theory-based account connects physical properties with physical theory; an object-based account starts from familiar physical objects and their parts. Both raise problems, including circularity and Hempel’s dilemma about whether “physics” means current or future physics. The entry then compares reductive and non-reductive physicalism, and a priori with a posteriori physicalism. Objections include the possibility that physical facts leave out qualia, intentionality, or abstract objects. Support comes from causal closure and methodological naturalism, though each argument has disputed premises.
key_ideas: Physicalism is a claim about the nature of reality. It is not merely the claim that every sentence can be translated into the language of physics.
The entry separates two interpretation questions: what counts as physical, and what relationship everything must have to the physical.
Supervenience says that physical duplicates cannot differ in mental, biological, or social features. Some philosophers think this is necessary for physicalism but not strong enough by itself.
Identity theories are stronger. Token identity concerns particular objects or events; type identity concerns kinds of properties. Type identity may struggle with multiple realizability.
Realization and grounding try to describe physical dependence without saying that every higher-level property is identical to a physical property.
Arguments against physicalism focus especially on conscious experience, meaning, and abstract objects. Arguments for it appeal to causal closure and the success or methods of natural science.
summaries.why_it_matters: Physicalism is a framework for asking how different parts of life fit into the same universe. It matters to debates about the mind because it asks whether consciousness and thought can depend completely on physical reality. It also shows why scientific explanation, philosophical explanation, and everyday descriptions may be related without being identical.

important_terms.definition: The view that everything is physical, or is related to physical features in the way required by the view.
Dependence between properties: changes in higher-level features require some change in the underlying physical features.
The idea that two things are literally one and the same thing.
The possibility that the same higher-level feature can be produced by physically different systems.
A relation in which a physical property makes another property possible by playing its causal or explanatory role.
The idea that one fact is true because of, or in virtue of, another fact.
The felt side of an experience, such as the way a color looks.
The feature of thoughts and language that makes them about things or represent situations.

questions_to_think_about: If a school team depends on its players, is the team identical to one player or to the group as a whole?
Could the same kind of pain occur in organisms with very different physical structures?
Does complete physical information include information about what an experience feels like?
What would make a social rule physical: its written words, the people following it, or something else?
Are dependence and identity different enough to support a non-reductive physicalism?
